title: Νέος ἄσωτος καὶ χελιδών
titleEn: The Spendthrift Young Man and the Swallow
part: The Spendthrift Young Man and the Swallow (Chambry 248 · Perry 169)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 248 (= Perry 169). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Νέος ἄσωτος καταφαγὼν τὰ πατρῷα, ἱματίου αὐτῷ μόνου περιλειφθέντος, ὡς ἐθεάσατο χελιδόνα παρὰ καιρὸν ἐλθοῦσαν, οἰόμενος ἤδη θέρος εἶναι, ὡς μηκέτι δεόμενος τοῦ ἱματίου, καὶ τοῦτο φέρων ἀπημπόλησεν.
sentences.tr: Neos asōtos kataphagōn ta patrōia, himatiou autōi monou perileiphthentos, hōs etheasato chelidona para kairon elthousan, oiomenos ēdē theros einai, hōs mēketi deomenos tou himatiou, kai touto pherōn apēmpolēsen.
sentences.l: A spendthrift young man, having devoured his father's goods, only a cloak having been left him, when he beheld a swallow that had come out of season, thinking that it was already summer, as no longer needing the cloak, carrying this too, sold it off.
sentences.i: A spendthrift young man had devoured his father's estate, and nothing was left him but a cloak; and when he saw a swallow that had come before its time, he supposed summer was already there, and reckoning he had no further need of the cloak, took that too and sold it.
sentences.n: The swallow's return was the ordinary sign that the season had turned, and the Greek proverb warns that one swallow does not make a spring — this fable is that proverb told out. παρὰ καιρόν is 'beside the season', out of its due time. ἱματίου … περιλειφθέντος is a genitive absolute, a noun and participle standing loose from the sentence to set the circumstances; and ὡς with the participle (ὡς μηκέτι δεόμενος) gives the reason as the young man's own, not the narrator's. The ἱμάτιον is the outer wrap, the one garment a man could not do without in winter.

sentences.t: Ὕστερον δὲ χειμῶνος ἐπιλαβόντος καὶ σφοδροῦ τοῦ κρύους γενομένου, περιιών, ἐπειδὴ εἶδε τὴν χελιδόνα νεκρὰν ἐρριγωμένην, ἔφη πρὸς αὐτήν· « Ὦ αὕτη, σὺ κἀμὲ καὶ σὲ ἀπώλεσας. »
sentences.tr: Hysteron de cheimōnos epilabontos kai sphodrou tou kryous genomenou, periiōn, epeidē eide tēn chelidona nekran errigōmenēn, ephē pros autēn· « Ō hautē, sy kame kai se apōlesas. »
sentences.l: But later, winter having come on and the cold having grown fierce, going about, when he saw the swallow dead and frozen stiff, he said to her: « You there, you have destroyed both me and yourself. »
sentences.i: Later, when winter set in and the cold turned bitter, he was walking about and saw the swallow lying dead and frozen stiff, and said to her: « You there — you have ruined me and yourself together. »
sentences.n: ἐρριγωμένην is the perfect participle of ῥιγόω, 'to be stiff with cold'; the perfect states the condition she is now in. κἀμέ is καὶ ἐμέ run together by crasis. Ὦ αὕτη is a blunt way of hailing someone, 'you there' — Greek addresses even a dead bird in the feminine, as χελιδών is a feminine noun.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος δηλοῖ ὅτι πάντα τὰ παρὰ καιρὸν δρώμενα ἐπισφαλῆ τυγχάνουσιν.
sentences.tr: Ho logos dēloi hoti panta ta para kairon drōmena episphalē tynchanousin.
sentences.l: The story shows that all things done out of season prove perilous.
sentences.n: τυγχάνω with an adjective is 'to prove to be, turn out'. ἐπισφαλής is what is liable to trip and fall. The neuter plural subject takes a plural verb here rather than the usual singular — Chambry's page, not an error to be corrected.
